speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head M of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government is, of course, a massive entity and it may not always be possible to have full visibility as to whether we achieve value-for-money in what we spend.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: At the same time, we must be mindful to strike a balance between the speed of responses versus ensuring governance and checks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Minister how does MOF ensure effective allocation and productive use of resources so that we maintain fiscal accountability and sustainability, even as we are faced with the increasingly complex challenges that cut across Ministry lines, for example, cybersecurity, or even the setting up of our community isolation facilities?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How are we ensuring that the Government spends prudently and appropriately on big-ticket items such as our infrastructure where we are expecting more spending to come?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What are MOF’s efforts to drive accountability for outcomes of spending, especially for significant spending in response to the COVID-19 crisis?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In rendering support and relief to our businesses, families and workers, it would require the Government and agencies to work with decisiveness, speed and with empowerment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Assistance and relief support need to be timely and thoughtful to be meaningful, and to serve its purpose.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How has MOF exercised agility and flexibility to flow assistance to businesses and citizens more expeditiously at the outset of the crisis and during the circuit breaker?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: IRAS, ACRA and Customs are key interfacing agencies for businesses and citizens.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: From time to time, I do receive feedback and appeal requests from my constituents to expedite approvals and to seek waivers from these agencies that come under MOF.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How is MOF working together with the businesses to develop innovative solutions and enhance productivity?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How has MOF increased partnership and co-creation with the community in delivering solutions?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Working from home and flexi-work arrangements become suddenly workable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Digital transactions, QR code, Zoom meeting, among others, is now the way to go for businesses and for individuals.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It has implications in Public Service and would require enhancements as to how public sector can serve and deliver services.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How is the public sector gearing up for greater adoption of digitalisation among our businesses and society?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the case of MOF, what has the Ministry done to build capabilities in areas such as finance, procurement, grants management, shared services and internal audit?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, unprecedented Government expenditure has been incurred in the fight against the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is important that proper controls, governance and accountability over the use of public funds are maintained, even as Government agencies react swiftly to the evolving pandemic situation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Most importantly, support measures should be fair and must reach targeted groups, especially vulnerable groups such as low-income workers and families who have been disproportionately affected by the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It was a lifeline to many companies, helping them keep local employees on payroll.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It was broad-based, benefiting all companies albeit at different support tiers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In some countries, such as Australia, eligibility for wage support only kicks in if business turnover drops by 30% due to the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst I appreciate it is easier to assess impact on hindsight, could the Minister share how the Government prioritised assistance and channelled funding support during the outbreak?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What was the rationale to provide JSS across the board?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How does the Government evaluate the return on investments for such support schemes?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What KPIs are used to track progress and success to ensure public funds are judiciously allocated?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How is MOF deploying technology and data as the key enablers for agencies to better plan, collaborate and deliver public services more efficiently and effectively?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To-date, there almost 40 fiscal councils worldwide concentrated among advanced economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis dates back to just after the end of the Second World War while the Congressional Budget Office which serves both Houses of the United States legislature was founded in 1974.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Others have more recent prominence but have, nevertheless, become rapidly influential.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Canada's Parliamentary Budget Officer was established in 2006.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The United Kingdom's Office for Budget Responsibility was formally constituted in 2010 and most fiscal councils within the EU were set up following the European Fiscal Compact in 2012.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, fiscal councils are independent and are expected to provide non-partisan assessments of the expected effects of policy on revenue and expenditure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As such, they serve as trusted public institutions that can help score, reform ideas and proposals to help ensure the economy's commitment to sustainable public finances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The support functions that fiscal councils offer include public assessments of fiscal plans and performance and evaluation of all provision of macro-economic and budgetary forecasts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While these functions may already be performed to some degree by MOF, MOF reports to the government of the day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, the fiscal council will provide advice and the key here is advice as they do not possess any formal power to determine the Budget to the whole of Parliament at their request.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As such, the Council will be available to scrutinise policy proposals offered by PAP backbenchers as well as Opposition parties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I should point out that a proposal to form an independent Office of Budget Responsibility was raised by Mr Low Thia Khiang of the Workers' Party in 2017's Committee of Supply debates, This proposal builds on that, detailing the functions of the proposed agency and its service to the full legislature, and underscore the distinct macro-economic environment of the day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is evidence that fiscal councils can improve fiscal performance, especially when such Councils enjoy legal and operational independence, are tasked with monitoring fiscal rules and are supported by a robust media presence.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Leon Perera, please, if you would like, take all three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, my first cut on National Research Foundation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The National Research Foundation is responsible for directing a huge amount of Government spending.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In other countries, we do hear anecdotally how government-supported R&D initiatives help seed IP to domestically based companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the US, for example, it is known that in the past, NASA might have seeded technology to American companies, technology that arose from the state-funded space effort.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I have spoken in the House about this before.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The nexus between state research institutes and research centres on the one hand and local companies on the other, is not non-existent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, some new initiatives were rolled out in 2018 to try to ease the process by which local firms can engage with the R&D capabilities residing in our RIs and RCs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, I still hear anecdotally that local firms find this process not altogether easy to navigate and that there is a perception that those local firms, able to write and present their proposals well or those that hire consultants, are best able to navigate this process as opposed to those with the best ideas.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is in line with one of the themes of my Budget debate speech that we should score an "A" for outcomes, not only an "A" for effort.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The two objectives, of course, are not mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The second cut on assessing the performance of sovereign wealth funds.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, Temasek and GIC, no doubt compare their performance against various global market indices and other standards of performance internally.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It would be useful for these Sovereign Wealth Funds (SWFs) to publish these comparisons in the analysis for the reasons for better assessment of their performance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, it would be useful for the Government in the form of MOF to understand these comparisons in some detail.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: With that said, I would like to ask how does the MOF itself assess that the SWFs Boards and management have done a reasonable job in terms of returns.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What internal metrics, indices and benchmarks and processes are used?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the case of Temasek, the MSCI is used as a reference.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It has argued that its under-performance relative to the risk adjusted cost of capital is because it is making a systemic shift to build resilience for the future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, the reserves consist of various classes of assets held by Temasek, GIC and the MAS, if we are to exclude land banks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: During typical economic crises some asset value such as equities may fall on the whole.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If a result draw-down is financed by liquidating assets in a time of crisis, this may not necessarily be advantageous for Singapore since it may mean selling fundamentally good assets, such as shares and good blue chip companies, for example, at low prices rather than hanging on to those assets to realise future value when the economy recovers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, if the reserves draw-down is financed by borrowing against the collateral of the reserves, that may in some circumstances prove to be more advantages to Singapore, especially given that interest rates may be lower in a time of global economic crisis as central banks slash the cost of credit to financial institutions as they often do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And in conclusion, I just like to add that I am aware that during the COVID-19 period, some sectors and some stock exchanges and market indices actually rose.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In that sense, this crisis has been atypical.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My comments earlier referred to more typical global economic crisis.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, as the Government continues to fiscally strategise to meet long-term needs of our nation through investing in essential sectors, I would like to suggest that the Government adopt more upstream urban design ideas to optimise downstream operating expenses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Organic waste is transported through a system of pipes to an onsite digester which could up-cycle waste into useful products.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a system reduces overall cleaning and haulage cost due to lesser need for point-to-point transportation, allowing for a reduction in carbon footprint too.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also would like to recommend training in deep sector technical knowledge for relevant public officers so that procurement tenders are scoped with the best outcome.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Creating more secondment opportunities for public officers to be attached to high growth Singapore businesses to gain first-hand experience would also be ideal.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having equipped with industry technical knowledge would allow for all translation work to be more effective, alongside with industry feedback and insights.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can find the balance of being both cost conscious and outcome driven and embrace the importance of design in our public services.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Chairman, the Government can play an active role to give local businesses a leg up.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: This will not only go a long way to bolster the vibrancy of our local merchants but to foster a strong spirit of community and solidarity.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: SingapoRediscover Vouchers is another excellent example of supporting local tourism at a time when they most needed it.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The key challenge based on feedback from my residents is in navigating the various participating websites to look for something of interest.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The current process of redemption seems time-consuming and complicated, especially to the less tech savvy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Government can support businesses better by flowing assistance to them more easily, staying nimble and customising support.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: To achieve flexibility and agility, Government will need to gain new capabilities in setting more dynamic parameters and monitoring mechanisms.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: This is especially relevant with respect to datasets and applications specific to Singapore as part of our digitalisation efforts.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: How can Government developed APIs be shared with local businesses to support fast track development of new commercial applications?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: What plans are there to foster a closer partnership and cocreation with the local businesses in delivering solutions?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, 2020 was a year fraught with challenges.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We saw an increased number of applications for financial assistance, be they from businesses or citizens.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Despite the wide array of support, I note that some have had to make appeals or request for further support.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They were not aware of what supporting information to provide, or were found to be narrowly ineligible.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister share how agility and flexibility have been exercised to avail assistance to businesses and citizens more quickly during COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And how are the involved personnel equipped to cope with the increased workload?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there a need to enhance their capabilities?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, there has been a growing global emphasis on Environmental, Social and Governance or ESG goals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This reflects expanded role of companies in driving our environmental and social outcomes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And there is still vast potential still to be tapped, especially for private companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Their customers and business partners can then better decide how their resources can used to pursue our environmental and social aims.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I understand that some companies have stayed privately held because of business considerations, some of which might be compliance requirements of public listing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, there are significant number of private companies compared to listed ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The latter which already have sustainability reporting requirements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Private companies can provide the added impetus for our Green Plan and gender diversity aims.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can strike a good balance by limiting to companies above a certain level of turnover or manpower size.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, can the Ministry also share on how Government grants are also used to drive sustainability and social outcomes?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Government share on its longer term plan to leverage on our procurement guidelines for good sustainability and gender diversity outcomes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Chairman, I am heartened by the growing passion and quality of debate inside and outside this House regarding our climate challenges.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Our sovereign wealth funds as global players should rightfully play a leading role in the effort to decarbonise.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We could kickstart this by having our Sovereign Wealth Funds (SWF) adopt the PSTLES style framework directed by MOF.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Can Temasek include scope 3's indirect emissions into its commitment since portfolio companies are often investors themselves?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: On GIC's end, we have no visibility in its portfolio environmental targets, will GIC release this information?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: While it may be impossible to disclose the full extent of investments, the declaration of standards companies must fulfil before a SWF can invest in them would be positive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Norway's SWF outlines concrete expectations of companies that it invests in and has an exclusion list on the types of companies that do not meet ethical and environmental standards.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: An explicit statement allows for accountability and sends a powerful message to the business community about what the Singapore brand stands for.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, with a 9% increase in private residential volumes in 2020 despite the absence of foreign buyers and despite COVID-19, the Singaporean aspirations of upgrading from public to private property is stronger than ever.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Enabling financially able Singaporeans to upgrade from HDB to private not only fulfils their aspirations, but it also eases demand for homes in the public residential market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD) has helped reduce excessive demand for property investments, it has also affected genuine HDB owners to upgrade to a private property.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given the rising prices of private property, 12% is no small amount, even though this could be remitted for married couples once they sell their first residential property within the specified timeline.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This experience is different for a HDB owner who upgrades to an Executive Condominium (EC) or even buying another larger HDB unit.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Mr Chairman, this remission reduces the pressure of having to pay the ABSD in a short span of 14 days, a relief the HDB owners transitioning to private properties do not enjoy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would MND explore harmonising this remission to this group of citizens who wish to fulfil their housing aspirations?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, with the transformation and changes that we are witnessing, the public sector too needs to build capability to stay relevant.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A key role that the public sector plays is that of steward of public resources.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With digitalisation and the pace of change, traditional Government procurement processes will need to evolve as current tender procurement processes may not always work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The effective use of technology and digitalisation enables agility, speed and the capability to do things differently.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How has MOF leveraged digitalisation to strengthen public sector capabilities and processes, to transform the way work is done and improve how citizen services are delivered?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Transforming public sector services is not just about application of technology or digitalising.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It involves relooking at how things are done and in some cases, completely new ways of doing things.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Digitalisation enabled by new technologies and platforms is also increasing citizen engagement and feedback with Government.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is changing the dynamics of citizen and Government engagement and will require public officers to have new mindsets, technology and leadership skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How is the public sector developing public officers, bringing in new talent and competencies and ensuring the retention of subject matter expertise?

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Members for their questions and comments for MOF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The cuts by Members cover four broad areas: first, fiscal sustainability and accountability; second, managing our investments and reserves and tax-related matters; third, supporting social and environmental outcomes; and fourth, supporting businesses, citizens and community and enhancing public service capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will speak on the first and second areas and my colleague, Second Minister for Finance Ms Indranee Rajah will cover the other two areas and the proposal for an independent fiscal council.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Ms Foo Mee Har raised important points and asked how the Government ensures prudent and effective allocation of resources, especially in such challenging times.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And I want to assure both Mr Liang and Ms Foo that we take these issues very seriously, especially on securing good value-for-money and good outcomes with the resources that we have.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we continually prioritise and reallocate funds to key areas of greater needs across the whole-of-Government so that it is not just about additional spending but also about re-prioritisation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, we have joint budgeting arrangements for cross-cutting domains, to better align priorities and reduce duplication of resources across different agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Joint budgets have been set up in the areas of jobs and skills, vaccines and therapeutics, Smart Nation and Digital Government as well as in Research, Innovation and Enterprise.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms Foo asked how we evaluate the return on investment for support schemes directed towards new areas of development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As with all Government programmes, we monitor the output and outcomes of our programmes and schemes to ensure that their purposes are met.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also review whether to scale, refine, or sunset programmes depending on their outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, for digitalisation programmes, we look at digital adoption rate and digital readiness across the sectors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For enterprise development programmes, we monitor the growth of benefiting companies like revenue, to holistically assess how well the scheme objectives are met.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For Research and Development or R&D, we continuously seek to refine the way by which we assess and monitor the impact of our investments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We currently track a basket of indicators, which include Business Expenditure on Research and Development, the number of successful start-ups supported by Research, Innovation and Enterprise or RIE programmes, and the number of research projects that are undertaken in collaboration with the industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In this regard, Mr Leon Perera asked about enhancing the economic impact of research spending.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is an area where we share common objectives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We too in MOF would like to enhance the economic impact of everything that we spend.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want to achieve an "A" score not just for effort but for outcomes too.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want to have "As" in all areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We continue to place a strong focus on ensuring that RIE investments develop the capabilities needed to catalyse economic growth.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, we recognise that some investments in basic research are essential and are important and they should continue to be maintained for laying the foundations of downstream breakthroughs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The nature of basic research is that they may not always have direct translational outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Or even if they do, the outcomes may take time to materialise and manifest themselves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, if you look at the American examples or even in Israel, some of the basic research is done with very little direct and immediate outcomes because the economic outcomes bear fruits many, many years later.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In Singapore, we have a similar example of our biomedical sciences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We started investing in R&D in biomedical science in 2000.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The initial years were not easy but we stayed the course.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We had patient capital and today, our investments have set the stage for the flourishing Biomedical Science (BMS) sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: RIE activities have also helped to catalyse private sector research and innovation activity and to establish a vibrant innovation and enterprise eco-system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The number of industry research scientists and engineers, or RSEs, has tripled.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Beyond the immediate impact on RSEs, RIE investments have also indirectly contributed to good jobs in the rest of the economy, by keeping industries and businesses competitive globally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, these are the outcomes that we have achieved and we will continually strive to do better.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In response to Mr Liang's question on accountability for spending outcomes, we continue to strengthen governance and accountability over the outcomes of our spending, including strengthening the value-for-money culture across all Government agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Infrastructure projects are evaluated for their worthiness and cost-effectiveness, before the Government embarks on them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For larger projects, Ministries' proposals and MOF's evaluations are further scrutinised by the Development Projects Advisory Panel, which comprises technical experts from the private sector and academia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, MOF worked with LTA to improve the proposed design for the Sengkang West multi-storey bus depot-cum-dormitory, including right-sizing the space for housing mechanical and electrical equipment and common areas, and green roof areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These changes helped to reduce the estimated cost by about $70 million.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For day-to-day operational spending, public agencies also proactively look out for ways to spend prudently.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I also thank Mr Edward Chia for his suggestion on making greater use of design to optimise cost effectiveness over the lifespan of infrastructure projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, the Government adopts a life-cycle cost perspective during upfront planning and in the design of infrastructure projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It allows us to optimise the combination of upfront costs and downstream maintenance and operating costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms Foo spoke about the need for governance and accountability over the use of public funds, even as we were responding to the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, when coming up with support schemes, agencies do make full use of a whole range of tools.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They considered the possibilities of fraud and unintended beneficiaries upfront in scheme designs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They deployed various monitoring mechanism and safeguards, at pre-disbursement and post-disbursement stages, to ensure that funds are disbursed to the appropriate beneficiaries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Specifically, on the Jobs Support Scheme (JSS), this was introduced at the start of the crisis when the public health and economic situation was highly fluid, and when firms were facing immediate cashflow issues.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The priority then was to ensure that all firms received timely support, so that they could focus on retaining their workers and sustaining their operations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The JSS was implemented as a broad-based scheme then, without the need for onerous applications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As the economic situation improved and with actual data on sectoral and firm performance, we then stepped down our broad-based support measures and pivoted towards more targeted, sector-specific measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, we began tapering JSS support levels from September 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For sectors that managed well, we ceased JSS support after December 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In this Budget, we extended the JSS for Tier 1 sectors like aviation and tourism by six months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For Tier 2 sectors like land transport and retail, we extended by three months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For sectors that remain hard hit, we also introduced additional targeted measures like the SingapoRediscovers Vouchers to stimulate domestic tourism, and extended sector-specific support like the Aviation, Point-to-Point Support Packages and the Arts and Culture Resilience Package.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This tiered approach has enabled us to bring targeted relief to business owners and the workers they are responsible for.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to monitor the outcomes and effectiveness of COVID-19-related schemes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, MOF has published its interim assessment of the initial effects of the Government's measures to reduce business costs, save jobs and support families.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, let me talk about managing our investments and reserves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Perera asked about the performance of our investment entities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have had this debate before, this question has been raised multiple times and I have explained that both GIC and Temasek are long-term investors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Their remit is to secure good sustainable returns on a total portfolio basis over the long term.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the relevant performance measure for them is not the year-to-year return which can fluctuate because of market volatility but sustained long-term returns over and above global inflation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If you look at that measure, both GIC and Temasek have indeed performed creditably over the long term.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Their results are published in their annual reports and there is a full writeup explaining their decisions, their performance and the evaluation of their performance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: GIC in recent years, has recognised that there is high uncertainty in the equity markets, as well as high valuations, which can lead to large permanent portfolio impairment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As a result, GIC has undertaken pre-emptive measures to reduce portfolio risks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Nevertheless, despite reducing its risk exposure, GIC's returns on its portfolio, compared to a reference portfolio comprising 65% equities and 35% bonds; GIC's performance, despite a reduced risk, has been equal, if not better, than the reference portfolio.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This has been so, over the rolling 20-year period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Going forward, how do we ensure that such performance continues?

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But all the processes are in place, by the Boards who supervise management, between MOF and the Boards to review the performances of these entities, and in discussions with external parties as well as investment advisory panels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Very prominent names in the investment community sit on these advisory panels to help us guide our two entities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Nevertheless, both entities acting on their own accord, emphasise sustainability in their investment activities, and that is because they recognise that good sustainability practices are good for business and can have a positive impact on long-term returns.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Conversely, companies with poor sustainability practices carry business and reputational, as well as environmental, social and governance risks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Both entities take a strong interest in not only understanding sustainability-related challenges, but also the opportunities for innovation, business growth and new investments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Both entities also support efforts by the Financial Stability Board's Task Force for Climate-related Financial Disclosures, or TCFD, to develop an internationally accepted framework on climate reporting.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This provides a framework for companies to disclose their climate-related strategies, and for investors to incorporate climate change considerations into long-term investment decisions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Both entities have also published comprehensive statements on their approach to sustainability and they will continue to review what additional information can be pulled out in their annual reports.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In response to Mr Perera's question about reserves spending, let me just explain how the Government executes the spending of reserves during economic crises.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The fiscal framework in the Constitution requires the Government to spend within its means.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister, if you would like to pause, we have arranged for some water.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not a bug, I assure you.

speaker: The Chairman
text: And we would not steal your time; the timer has stopped.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is part of the Government's overall cash flow management.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is an operational issue and is separate from the budgeting process.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For purposes of cash flow management, the Government has a range of liquidity sources it can tap on, and this would include tax revenues which come in at different times of the year, funds raised outside the Budget, like proceeds from land sales.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Constitutionally they do not contribute to the Budget and do not count as Government revenues, but they are part of the cash flow that the Government receives.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It also includes Government deposits which we can draw on for purposes of cash flow reasons.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, all of these cash flows are pooled together and all of the sources of liquidity are pooled together and we manage cash flow on a disciplined and integrated basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On top of these different sources, I have highlighted earlier in this House that the Government will be issuing Cash Management Treasury Bills.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is part of the Government's ongoing efforts to expand our cash management tool kit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, GIC was not put in a position where it had to liquidate investments under time pressure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The aim of ABSD, I think we all know, is to moderate demand and to ensure a stable and sustainable residential property market.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: To be effective as a measure to moderate demand for property, ABSD has to be applied consistently and to all buyers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Only one exception is made, namely that is for Singaporean married couples.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A Singaporean married couple may need to change homes due to changing family needs, such as when they have children, when their children are growing up, or when the couple needs to right-size in their senior years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is in this context that we have an ABSD concession for Singaporean married couples buying a second residential property.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For those who are purchasing a HDB flat or a new Executive Condominium, they are granted upfront ABSD remission, as Mr Chua highlighted.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is because, they are subject to HDB regulations which require them to not own another residential property and to dispose of their existing property within HDB's stipulated timeframe.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are no such regulations for private residential properties and that is the reason why for such private residential property purchases, ABSD remission is only granted upon the sale of the first property within the required timeline, unlike the case of HDB.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Second Minister Ms Indranee will now address the other questions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Pritam Singh had suggested a Parliamentary Budget Office.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In his response, the Deputy Prime Minister had referred to that as having a $20 million budget being requested for it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Hence, I sought clarification from the Leader of the Opposition whether his Parliamentary Budget Office was the same as the independent fiscal council and the Leader of the Opposition kindly confirmed that they were actually the same.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There is only one council that he is talking about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And we heard Assoc Prof Jamus Lim just now, who has confirmed that what he is asking is for a council that is set up at a proposed cost of $20 million.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is just so that everybody knows what everyone is speaking about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, let me address Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's cut.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In assessing the value of such a proposal, the fundamental starting point must always be: why?

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Assoc Prof Jamus Lim ran us through various independent fiscal entities around the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will refer to them as Independent Fiscal Institutions, or IFIs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, it is important to first understand the context in which such institutions are established.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There were some which were established beforehand, for example, in the US and the Netherlands, but, primarily, the largest bulk of them were established after the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, more than half of the IFIs in the OECD today were established after the Global Financial Crisis and the main intent was to prevent future fiscal crises.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In those cases, fiscal rules had proved insufficient to ensure prudent management of the public finances before the crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: IFIs were set up to safeguard fiscal discipline, eradicate unreliable budgeting and rebuild public trust in policy-makers' capacity to manage public budgets prudently and transparently.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, the context in Singapore is very different.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are among the small number of countries today that continue to enjoy a AAA credit rating.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government has been disciplined in keeping to our fiscal rules and safeguards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have run balanced Budgets in each term of Government, barring major crises.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The draw on past reserves for COVID-19 relief, which was a crisis situation, was done in accordance with our Reserves Protection Framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have put in place a strong system to scrutinise spending and debate budgetary matters, without incurring the costs of setting up additional fiscal monitoring institutions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Constitution requires us to run a balanced Budget over each term of Government and any departure would require the approval of the President.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government is required under the Constitution to seek Parliament's approval for its expenditure and revenue during each year's Budget.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The annual Budget Debate and Committee of Supply (COS) provide the opportunity for Members of Parliament to debate on and scrutinise Government policies and programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under the Constitution, the Government cannot draw on the reserves accumulated by past terms of Government without the approval of the elected President.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There is a standing Parliamentary Select Committee, the Estimates Committee, which examines the Government's Budget.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government's accounts are audited by the Auditor-General's Office.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The AGO's findings are reported to the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), also another Parliamentary Committee, which can call on the relevant agencies to explain lapses or take corrective actions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: More importantly, the Government has been upfront about the hard choices that we make on budgetary matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, we have not shied away from highlighting the need to raise taxes to meet longer term increase in healthcare and social spending needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Robust, intellectually honest analysis is important to foster more informed parliamentary debate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But ultimately, there is no substitute for having the political courage to make difficult budgetary choices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Members of an independent fiscal council are not elected representatives in Parliament.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Their role is to advise, but the responsibility for making difficult decisions ultimately lies with the elected Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Alice Rivlin, the founding chair of the US Congressional Budget Office, said this very well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She said that IFIs, I quote, "can play an important role in ensuring realistic and well-informed debate based on honest numbers, focusing attention on the consequences of action (or inaction), and identifying more or less sustainable solutions to budget dilemmas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They cannot instil political courage to make unpopular decisions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Political leaders have to do that for themselves".

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It will also not miraculously remove the structural drivers for higher healthcare and social expenditure, nor will it delay any painful changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Based on the experience of other countries, did the setting up of IFIs solve their fiscal management issues?

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: No, because, ultimately, we cannot outsource honest and upfront debate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We should focus our time and our energy on having robust, honest and constructive debates, deciding on the trade-offs and not delegate that responsibility to a third party.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We recognise that there will always be uncertainty in forecasting and fiscal planning, but we cannot wish away more fundamental drivers of expenditure, particularly the increase in public health expenditure, as our population ages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, I move on now to address some of the other cuts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On supporting social and environmental outcomes, Mr Desmond Choo asked how we can drive environmental and social outcomes through our funding and corporate regulatory levers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOF allocates public resources, and uses tax, charges and corporate regulatory levers, in order to achieve broader societal objectives, including social and environmental outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have more than doubled our spending in the social and environmental sectors over the last decade, and we have achieved good social outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the area of gender equality, Singapore reports our progress regularly to the United Nations Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have done relatively well in areas such as higher education attainment, and are closing the gender gap in labour force participation rates and wages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In some metrics, such as women in corporate leadership, we still lag behind the most progressive countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Women still shoulder most of the care-giving burden.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For environmental outcomes, we have one of the lowest carbon emissions per dollar of GDP in the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Building on this, we are working towards peaking our emissions around 2030, and achieving our long-term net-zero aspirations as soon as viable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To do so, we are supporting businesses and households to become more energy-efficient, among other initiatives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On procurement, environmental sustainability requirements are already part of the consideration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For instance, agencies are required to buy energy-efficient appliances, and Government buildings are required to achieve Green Mark standards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will continue to enhance these requirements in support of GreenGov.SG.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Choo also suggested using the corporate regulatory lever.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are existing disclosure requirements for listed companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, the Code of Corporate Governance requires listed companies to disclose their board diversity policy in the company's annual report.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Singapore Exchange (SGX) Listing Rules require listed companies to prepare annual sustainability reports.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government is mindful that a unified international sustainability framework has yet to be agreed upon and is monitoring international developments closely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will take these into account in studying when it would be feasible and timely to introduce sustainability reporting for non-listed companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Besides the efforts made by the Government, businesses, organisations and individuals must all play their part in changing their mindsets and accepting new societal norms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I encourage the various stakeholders to step up and help us achieve better environmental and social outcomes together.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I move on now to the other cuts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how MOF exercised agility and flexibility to flow assistance quickly to businesses and citizens.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In response to COVID-19, our priority was to flow assistance to those affected as quickly as possible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The JSS has helped to keep our unemployment rate in check.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also facilitated faster payment to Government suppliers to ease their cashflows.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: During the pandemic, we went the extra mile to pay businesses as early as possible, rather than when the payment is due, which is typically 30 days from the invoice date.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We exercised flexibility in applying regulations on businesses in view of the COVID-19 disruptions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority, or ACRA, extended the deadline to hold Annual General Meetings (AGMs) and file annual returns for companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ACRA also worked closely with MAS, Singapore Exchange Regulation and other agencies to facilitate virtual AGMs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: An estimated 120,000 eligible companies can benefit from this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Saktiandi also asked how we coped with the increased workload.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Public Service mobilised manpower resources within and across agencies to help our frontline operations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On top of that, we also hired temporary staff.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I agree with Ms Foo Mee Har that it is important for the Government to step up our collaborations and increase partnership to co-create solutions with businesses and the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Agencies considered the suggestions and refined our support scheme parameters to benefit more citizens and businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, I notice that my time will be running out, and I do have a little more to cover.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Since we are still within the guillotine time, may I have your permission to continue?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are stepping up our partnerships with businesses, community groups and citizens to create policy solutions together.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, the Technology Hub for Non-Profit Organisations (NPO) initiative, was an idea that originated from the NPO leaders to accelerate the digital transformation of the non-profit sector during COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Tote Board partnered MCCY, MSF and NCSS and worked with IT companies to put together this one-stop shop, providing a variety of shared-service IT manpower, programmes and digital solutions to NPOs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Edward Chia and Ms Jessica Tan asked about MOF's efforts in building up public sector capabilities and strengthening functional leadership.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MOF is leading efforts to raise public sector capabilities in essential functions, such as finance, procurement, grants management, shared services and internal audit.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These functions play vital roles in ensuring the Government spends prudently, effectively and accountably.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When these functions perform well, agencies can focus on their core missions of helping businesses, citizens and the community.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MOF has re-organised ourselves and formed dedicated offices to drive these efforts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Grants Governance Office was formed to drive its implementation and raise agencies' capabilities to ensure proper financial governance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are transforming Government procurement to buy more smartly and effectively.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are taking further steps to consolidate the procurement of facilities management services of Government buildings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A central team with deeper expertise would manage these premises, instead of smaller, decentralised teams.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This provides the scale for service providers to adopt more innovative, less manpower intensive solutions to manage the facilities, and is in line with our industry transformation efforts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It also enabled the adoption of innovative technology solutions that facilitate workflow automation, data analytics and access to real-time data, which has improved service delivery at reduced costs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Mr Chia pointed out, we need to develop public officers with deep sector technical knowledge.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Finance and Procurement Academy set up by MOF is working with agencies such as the Building and Construction Authority and GovTech to deepen technical know-how in specialised procurement areas such as contract management for construction and Infocomm Technology.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will also be facilitating attachment stints and exchange programmes with the private sector to enable our officers to stay abreast of the latest professional and industry developments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In response to Ms Foo and Ms Tan's questions, as we strengthen the public sector capabilities and processes, we are also adopting more pervasive digitalisation in our processes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These efforts also help spur digital transformation in the private sector.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are currently piloting this with Eezee and Shopee, and will be onboarding more e-commerce platforms progressively in the coming months.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This solution not only helps us save processing time, it also incentivises vendors to digitalise and bring their businesses online.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Foo also asked if local businesses could re-use Government developed capabilities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Minister Vivian Balakrishnan earlier mentioned various collaborations between Government and the private sector, like SGFinDex, to deliver solutions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: GovTech has also launched the Singapore Government Developer Portal in December 2020.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This one-stop resource site enables tech developers to discover the latest Government IT solutions to build on and integrate into their applications.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, in conclusion, the Public Service continues to enhance its capabilities, and is committed to working with the community and businesses to position Singapore to grow and thrive for the long term.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Let us work in partnership so that Singapore can emerge stronger together.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: As we battled the COVID-19 crisis and the public sector had to respond almost on the move and to make time critical decisions, and probably with no SOP manual to reference from, whether it is to set up the massive community isolation facilities or with the under urgency of time for the foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: These are all unprecedented things that the public sector did last year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: We know that MOF does have very strict procurement policies and processes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: I read a lot of this in the AGO reports where the lapses were picked up and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: So, in the situation such as this, with the urgency and the exigencies, needs, how has our procurement process been able to allow for such situations to be managed?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: And then, whether there is the provision of waivers and so on for such acts?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Liang for the question.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, this was raised last year too, when we were in the midst of, well, we still are in the midst, of fighting COVID-19, but at the height of the pandemic last year when we had a huge outbreak.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think since then, the situation is more stable.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Agencies are able to respond in a much more coordinated and effective manner, but we never take anything for granted because the situation is highly unpredictable and new threats, new challenges may always emerge over the horizon.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And would not a second opinion on how our fiscal prospects are going forward into the future be valued, especially, as I emphasised in my cut, that this would be in the form of advisory nature rather than as law?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The second point that I thought would be useful to point out is that in the proposal, I had indicated that the independent fiscal council would actually serve all of this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And so, if by implication, does that mean that we should regard all proposals by all Members of this House as equally, fiscally credible that whatever estimates provided should be regarded as equally trustworthy as long as they are put on the table.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, in part, you can think of it as not purely a constraint on the Government, which does have a very good track record, as I have explained, but also on proposals that are offered by Members of this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: They may not have enjoyed as long and illustrious a track record.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Member for his clarification.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am sorry, I did not understand the second clarification.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Could the Member repeat it or explain it in clearer terms?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, my question was if the Minister or the Ministry believes that in the absence of such a fiscal council, are all suggestions about policy, even if it is self scored by us, and not by an independent fiscal council would be treated with the same regard?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the hon Member for his clarification.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the first one he asked whether I thought that the macroeconomic fiscal environment is unchanged and whether or not a second opinion would be valued.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the first one, of course, it has changed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So yes, it has changed, but the important thing is this – what is the difference between Singapore and the other countries who have needed the IFIs or their own fiscal councils?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They would not raise taxes when they needed to.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some did not display the political courage that was needed in order to maintain a balanced budget.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Singapore on the other hand – thanks to the foresight of our pioneering PAP leaders – set aside our reserves, refused to squander the reserves, put in place a constitutional framework which required us to run a balanced Budget and to make sure that any time that we had to dip into the reserves, it was for good reason and put in place a framework where you could use the income on the reserves, but set in place a certain limit.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All of these things are what set Singapore apart, and that is one of the reasons why we do not need a financial council like this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And earlier on in his answer, the hon Member referred to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in the UK and referenced a cut made by Mr Low Thia Khiang some years ago.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The hon Member was not in the House at that time, but I would like to read out an excerpt of what I had responded to Mr Low at that time, which is still relevant today.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When the OBR in the UK was set up, it was done so by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the Rt Hon George Osborne, and this is what he said when he set up the OBR, because it was set up by the Tory government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He said, "Over the last 13 years, the public and the markets have completely lost confidence in government economic forecasts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Unsurprisingly, these forecasting errors have almost always been in the wrong direction.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We need long-lasting change in the way we put together budgets in this country.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The final decision on the forecast has always been made by the Chancellor, not independent officials.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Again and again, the temptation to fiddle the figures, to nudge up a growth forecast here or reduce a borrowing number there to make the numbers add up has proved too great...We need to fix the budget to fit the figures and not fix the figures to fit the budget.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To do this, I am today establishing a new independent Office for Budget Responsibility.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For the first time, we will have a truly independent assessment of the state of the nation's finances." That was the scenario that prompted the setting up of the OBR.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That scenario is not present in Singapore, and for that, we have very good civil servants and agencies to thank, who keep us straight, who keep us narrow, who keep us honest.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And he asked whether a second opinion is valued.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Well, I have explained firstly why it is not necessary.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But I also want to go on to point out that in the UK, after setting up the OBR, it has not necessarily been the case that they have been on target.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the second opinion, well, in 2012, the OBR admitted it had a poor forecasting record.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The OBR had predicted economic growth six times stronger than the latest official figures suggested.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And in August 2020, the Institute for Fiscal Studies or the IFS described the OBR's "upside scenario" economic forecasts for UK GDP as "extraordinarily optimistic".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, second opinion does not always settle the issue.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With regard to the second clarification, the learned Member said that the council he is proposing will serve the full Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The suggestion really is that, okay, this is going to be for everybody.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And he asked whether in the absence of such a fiscal council, all suggestions will be treated with the same regard.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Well, the Parliament comprises the Members of Parliament who form the Government, the Members of Parliament who are part of the Ruling Party's backbenchers and the Opposition Members of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Insofar as proposals are put forward by the Government, these are assessed by the Civil Service.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government has an idea of the costing of its proposals and how it should be dealt with.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The first one is on the National Research Foundation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think the Minister referred to some of the downstream outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: For example, four of the top 10 blockbuster drugs in the world are manufactured in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I believe those four are by MNCs though.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, my question would be, really, in terms of local companies, locally owned companies, does the NRF actually track the IP that its spending has resulted in, the IP that is co-created with local companies, and does it track whether that IP then is used to create a blockbuster drug or a blockbuster product by the local company itself further downstream?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Is that something that the NRF looks at?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I accept, of course, that there are different uses for research, not just one.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But is that dimension kind of being tracked or will it be tracked, going forward?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I know that these results take time to manifest.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I believe NRF was set up in 2002 or 2003, so it has been 17 or 18 years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, I am wondering if that is being tracked, examples of that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, my question is, really, that the Government in the form of MOF is the sole shareholder, basically, of GIC and Temasek, and as the sole shareholder, is there a process within the MOF where you assess whether their performance is good enough?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In past debates on this subject, I believe that the Government has said its approach is a bit hands-off; it leaves it to the Board and management.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But I am wondering whether there is a formal process every year or every few years to assess whether the Board and management have done well or whether they have done not well enough, so that they need to be taken to task or, in extremis, whether they need to be replaced.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Does that sort of happen within MOF or somewhere else in the Government?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Chairman, let me take the two questions from Mr Perera.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It takes longer, understandably, because the capabilities of our local firms may not be at the same level as MNCs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, their readiness to take research and to translate research into tangible outcomes may not quite be there.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, there is an on-going effort to transform industries to boost the capabilities of our local firms.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But a second prong of this is through NRF's research initiatives itself, some of these get translated into local start-ups, and then these start-ups, in the nature of start-ups, not every one will succeed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some may exit early but we certainly hope some of them, over time, will grow and be very successful companies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And because we are still relatively early in this journey, I think we do need patience.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Just to give an example of a successful start-up like that which came from research in one of our universities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This was a project that started from a R&D project in NTU, I think, in 1999; that long ago.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is the kind of gestation periods that we are talking about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are tracking this; we are certainly wanting more translational outcomes that will benefit our economy and local firms.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I ask for patience from everyone, even as we track this effort on a continuing basis and strive for better outcomes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is a whole range of processes that we have put in place to do this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First of all, oversight by the Boards which they ought to do as part of their fiduciary duties.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Both entities have advisory panels, as I have highlighted, and that also provides guidance and oversight.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MOF itself has a review process where we meet the Board and management of Temasek on a regular basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We get them to update us on their understanding of the overall scenario, the risks, the outlook and opportunities they can envisage over the horizon, and what kinds of investment strategies they have in mind.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And then on top of all that, at the end of the day, it all comes down to the returns, and based on the risks that they are taking, the returns that they are delivering.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I have highlighted, we look at these returns not just on a yearly basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think that would be very short-sighted and that would be detrimental and counter-productive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That they are able to deliver consistently good returns over the longer term.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, do you wish to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: And I am sure behind each of these extensive series of well-structured and thoughtful Budget measures, there were a lot of hard work put in by the officers, the brain-crunching, the deliberations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: I think no amount of Auntie Mei Jok's porridge can make up for it.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: With that, Sir, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
